<article class="proj">

<div class="proj-layout">

<div class="proj-glance">
<p class="glance-role"><i class="bi bi-person-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>First author</p>
<ul class="glance-tags" aria-label="Scale and methods"><li>Present-value framework</li><li>Developer, ratepayer, social ledgers</li><li>Illustrative 300 MW-IT case</li><li>Latin hypercube screening</li><li>Staged service, bridge power</li></ul>
</div>
<section class="proj-q" aria-labelledby="h-question">
<h2 id="h-question"><i class="bi bi-question-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Research question</h2>
<p class="proj-question">What does it cost when a large AI data center must wait for grid energization, and how does the delay affect the developer, electricity ratepayers and society?</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-insight" id="insight" aria-labelledby="h-insight">
<h2 id="h-insight"><i class="bi bi-stars" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key insight</h2>
<p class="insight-title">The cost of delayed energization depends on who is counting</p>
<p>A late grid connection costs the developer lost margin and carrying costs; ratepayers face utility carrying and stranding costs; society bears external costs. I keep these present-value accounts separate. In the study&#x27;s illustrative base case, a 36-month delay for a 300 MW-IT facility cost the developer on the order of $0.7 billion, while ratepayer exposure depended strongly on large-load tariff design.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-contribution">
<h2 id="h-contribution"><i class="bi bi-person-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>My contribution</h2>
<p>First author. I did most of the work: the framework, the model, the analysis and the writing.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" id="approach" aria-labelledby="h-approach">
<h2 id="h-approach"><i class="bi bi-tools" aria-hidden="true"></i>How I approached it</h2>
<ol class="approach">
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>Delay costs fall on different parties, and a single total hides who pays.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I priced the delay in three separate present-value ledgers (developer, utility ratepayers and society) with a net-benefit test that states when they may be combined.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>An acceleration option can then be judged against what it saves each party and what it costs.</p></li>
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>Delay costs of projects with different sizes and waits are hard to compare.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I defined two metrics: a delay cost intensity per MW-month, and a break-even acceleration payment for options that shorten the wait.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>They make results comparable across project sizes, delays and mitigation options such as staged service or bridge power.</p></li>
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>Inputs are uncertain, and the length of a delay and whether a project goes ahead may be linked.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I screened inputs with Latin hypercube sampling and rank correlations, and stress-tested the dependence between delay and realization and the large-load tariff.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>The parameters are illustrative, so the study reports which inputs move the result, not a single forecast.</p></li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" id="choices" aria-labelledby="h-choices">
<h2 id="h-choices"><i class="bi bi-signpost-split" aria-hidden="true"></i>Design choices</h2>
<dl class="choices">
<div class="choice"><dt>Treat the delay as given</dt><dd><span class="ch-alt">Alternatives considered: modeling the interconnection process that causes it</span>The framework prices the consequences of late service; why service is late, and network feasibility, are outside its scope.</dd></div>
</dl>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-method">
<h2 id="h-method"><i class="bi bi-diagram-3" aria-hidden="true"></i>Method</h2>
<p>Present-value framework that converts delayed IT capacity into grid capacity requirements and prices the delay in separate developer, ratepayer and social ledgers, summarized by a delay cost intensity and a break-even acceleration payment; sensitivity and dependence stress tests.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-findings">
<h2 id="h-findings"><i class="bi bi-lightbulb" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key findings</h2>
<ol class="findings">
<li>In the study&#x27;s illustrative base case, a 36-month delay for a 300 MW-IT facility cost the developer on the order of $0.7 billion in present value.</li>
<li>Staged energization can recover a large share of that cost.</li>
<li>Ratepayer exposure depends strongly on large-load tariff design.</li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec proj-bounds" aria-labelledby="h-bounds">
<h2 id="h-bounds"><i class="bi bi-exclamation-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Boundary conditions</h2>
<p>The delay is treated as exogenous and parameters are illustrative; network feasibility is not modeled, and the social perspective is illustrated with a single bridge-power example.</p>
</section>
